input: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent, and the design predicts a recovery of 93% of the acetic acid in the feed. The solvent selection rests on the distribution coefficient, defined as the concentration of acetic acid in the organic phase divided by its concentration in the aqueous phase at equilibrium; the coefficient is 0.53 at 25 °C. A coefficient below unity means the aqueous phase holds the acid more strongly than the solvent takes it up, and recovery is reached by staging rather than by a single contact. The design uses 5 countercurrent stages, in which the solvent meets progressively weaker aqueous streams and leaves in contact with the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages: each stage is taken to reach the equilibrium distribution, so the stage count in the calculation is the stage count in the column. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility, with no solvent carried out in the raffinate and no water carried into the extract. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. A stage that falls short of equilibrium delivers less transfer than the calculation credits to it, and mutual solubility, where it occurs, removes solvent with the raffinate and dilutes the extract, and solvent lost to the raffinate must be recovered downstream or made up, at a cost the present design does not carry. The 93% figure is a design prediction on the stated assumptions, adequate for sizing the column and the solvent circulation; it is not a measured recovery, and a guarantee would need stage-efficiency and solubility data on the solvents as supplied.
